results.summary: This design takes two binary inputs and displays the corresponding decimal digit 0-3 on a 7-segment display. It is intended for use with an external LED display and switches, and can be tested by toggling the two input switches. The project is a simple educational example created in Wokwi. It has minimal documentation but clearly describes its function.

This design implements a 2-bit full adder that outputs a 3-bit sum on specific segments of a 7-segment display, and includes a clock divider that toggles the decimal point at a low frequency. It is tested by applying input combinations and observing the corresponding segment outputs according to a provided truth table. The design requires an external 7-segment display and switches for inputs. It is a simple educational project built in Wokwi.

This design is an 8-bit Fibonacci linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates a pseudorandom sequence of 255 non-zero states. It is tested by pulsing the reset signal and observing the 8-bit output patterns over successive clock cycles. No external hardware is required. The project is a straightforward implementation created during a TinyTapeout workshop.

This design uses a clock divider and multiplexers to alternate between displaying the designer's initials on a 7-segment display. It is controlled by a switch input and requires an external 7-segment display. The documentation provides no test procedure, stating 'Who needs tests?'. It is a simple personal project built in Wokwi.

This design implements a first-order sigma-delta analog-to-digital converter and a simple digital-to-analog converter, allowing an analog signal to be converted to a 1-bit digital stream and back to analog. It is intended for audio experimentation, with the input connected to an analog source and the output to an amplifier. External RC components are required for the analog front-end, and the design is noted to be crude and likely to add noise. The project is a basic exploration of sigma-delta modulation in Wokwi.

This design is a single flip-flop built from four NAND gates. It can be tested by toggling the input switches and observing the outputs, which are intended to drive two external LEDs. The documentation is very brief, stating only that it works and to try the switches. It is a minimal educational logic circuit created in Wokwi.

This design is a UART transmitter that continuously sends the string 'SHAOKAI'. It is tested by connecting the output to a serial receiver and verifying that the correct characters are printed. The design is based on a UART transmitter from the TinyTapeout website and requires an external serial receiver. The documentation is minimal, with no details on baud rate or configuration.

This design implements a simple Snake game on a 7-segment display, where a 3-segment snake moves around the display. The speed is controlled by an 8-bit input, and the direction is randomized using an LFSR. It requires only the 7-segment display on the demo board and is tested by supplying a 10 kHz clock and setting the speed. The design is a straightforward Wokwi example with a known limitation when changing speeds.

This design is a 7-segment display controller with minimal documentation. It has 6 input pins and 3 output pins, and is tested by clicking buttons. The description states only 'it works' and 'click the buttons'. The project lacks sufficient detail to determine its exact function or usage.

This design is described as a first chip for testing and learning, with a 60 Hz clock and 8 input and output pins. The documentation is extremely sparse, stating only 'Press play' and 'Test well'. It requires an external LED display. There is insufficient information to determine what the design actually does.
